grammar: The numeral is built units first: שְׁתַּיִם וְשִׁשִּׁים שָׁנָה וּמְאַת שָׁנָה, 'two and sixty years and a hundred years'.
וַיּוֹלֶד is Hifil wayyiqtol of ילד; the Hifil is the regular verb for a father's begetting.
The etnaḥta on שָׁנָה (second) divides the verse between the age and the birth.

grammar: אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ is a preposition plus infinitive construct with suffix: 'after his fathering'.
שְׁמֹנֶה מֵאוֹת: 'eight hundreds', the feminine numeral with the plural of מֵאָה.

The revia on יֶרֶד and the zaqef qaton on חֲנוֹךְ mark off the time clause אַחֲרֵי הוֹלִידוֹ אֶת־חֲנוֹךְ (the pashta on אַחֲרֵי is a minor division inside it); the etnaḥta on שָׁנָה closes the first half.
segments.note: The English keeps the Hebrew order of clauses by setting the time clause between commas.

commentary.summary: Onkelos renders literally (תַּמְנֵי מְאָה שְׁנִין, בְּנִין וּבְנָן).

grammar: וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ is Hitpael: 'walked about, walked habitually', here of a way of life.
אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים: אֶת here is the preposition 'with', so 'walked with God', not an object marker.
The formula 'and he lived' is replaced by 'and he walked with God': the change marks Enoch.
The three hundred years run from the birth of Methuselah, not from Enoch's birth.
segments.note: Ibn Ezra reads the walking as following God, like 'you shall walk after the LORD your God' (Deut 13:5); 'with God' keeps the preposition's plain sense. Radak, who is not normative, dates the beginning of Enoch's devotion to the sixty-fifth year.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra says 'he walked with God' has the sense of 'after the LORD your God you shall walk' (Deut 13:5), and compares Noah, 'with God Noah walked' (6:9), noting that some take 'Noah walked' as 'was accustomed'. The English 'walked with God' takes it as a way of life.
Onkelos: 'Enoch walked in the fear of the LORD' (וְהַלִּיךְ חֲנוֹךְ בְּדַחַלְתָּא דַּיְיָ); a paraphrase that the English does not adopt but that agrees in sense.
Sforno: he walked in God's ways, doing good to others by righteousness and by reproof; a further specification not in the text.

Unlike the other entries there is no וַיָּמֹת: the expected 'and he died' is missing.
The sum, 365, is the shortest in the chapter.
segments.note: The omission of 'and he died' is stated in the notes at 5:24.

'took him God'; verb first, then the pronominal object, then the subject

grammar: וְאֵינֶנּוּ is the particle אֵין with a suffix: 'and he was not'. It is a verbless clause.
לָקַח אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים: verb, pronoun object, then noun subject. A pronoun object regularly comes before a noun subject, so the order is the ordinary one and gives no special stress.
The etnaḥta on הָאֱלֹהִים closes the first half; the zaqef gadol on וְאֵינֶנּוּ separates the disappearance from its reason.
The first אֱלֹהִים has the article (the true God); the second does not, and is the subject.
segments.note: Rashi and Ibn Ezra agree that וְאֵינֶנּוּ ... לָקַח means that Enoch died, and the English 'he was no more, for God took him' carries that reading. They differ on its character: for Rashi a death before his time, for Ibn Ezra a death without plague or 'and he died', a taking 'with glory' (Ps 73:24). Radak records the view of the Targum and some sages that Enoch entered Eden alive; it is not the plain sense.

commentary.summary: Rashi (from Genesis Rabbah): Enoch was righteous but easily moved to turn to wickedness (קַל בְּדַעְתּוֹ לָשׁוּב לְהַרְשִׁיעַ), so God hastened to remove him and made him die before his time. That is why the text writes his death differently, וְאֵינֶנּוּ: he was not in the world to fill out his years (וְאֵינֶנּוּ בָּעוֹלָם לְמַלְּאוֹת שְׁנוֹתָיו).
Rashi: 'he took him' means before his time, as in 'I am taking from you the desire of your eyes' (Ezek 24:16). The English 'took him' keeps the sense of removal.

Ibn Ezra: וְאֵינֶנּוּ means he died, like 'take my life' (Jonah 4:3) and 'I am taking from you the desire of your eyes' (Ezek 24:16); but here there is no mention of a plague or of 'and he died', and the sense is that of 'afterward you will take me with honor' (Ps 73:24) and 'God will redeem my soul ... for he will take me' (Ps 49:16). The English 'he was no more, for God took him' leaves the manner open.

Radak: God took his soul and raised it to the upper beings, as in Ps 73:24 and 49:16; but the Targum and some sages say that Enoch and Elijah entered the garden of Eden alive in body and soul. The English does not choose.

Onkelos: 'Enoch walked in the fear of the LORD, and he was not, for the LORD caused him to die' (אֲמֵית יָתֵהּ יְיָ). The fetched text brackets a לָא, the reading of other editions: 'for the LORD did not cause him to die'.

apparatus: Enoch's departure is described by the verb לָקַח, 'take'; the verse does not say 'and he died'.
